analysis.investment_thesis: IDBI Bank is a recovering government-owned institution that has dug itself out of a severe NPA crisis, but nine years of near-zero revenue growth and sub-15% ROE leave no room to call this a wonderful business. The overhanging privatisation saga — promoter holding sits at a stifling 94.72% — has suppressed the stock for years, and a Forward P/E of 15.32 implies the market expects current earnings to deteriorate.
key_strengths: Remarkable NPA cleanup: losses of INR 14,970 Cr in FY19 reversed to INR 7,656 Cr net profit in FY25, a genuine operational turnaround
Balance sheet has grown — total assets from INR 300,699 Cr (FY20) to INR 416,730 Cr (FY25) — and capital base (equity) nearly doubled in five years
P/B of 1.16x is modest for a bank that now generates positive ROE, offering limited downside if privatisation proceeds
key_risks: Revenue CAGR of just 0.3% over nine years — the franchise has not grown; it has merely stopped shrinking
ROE of 13.6% is below my 15% minimum for a bank with this risk history; ROCE of 6.78% reflects the asset-heavy nature of banking
Privatisation by the Government of India and LIC (94.72% combined) is years behind schedule — capital locked in overhang, no catalysts visible
red_flags: Forward P/E of 15.32 vs trailing P/E of 8.69 implies the market models a ~43% earnings decline — something is not adding up
Negative operating cash flow in both FY23 (-INR 2,701 Cr) and FY24 (-INR 1,252 Cr), with FY25 OCF of INR 25,796 Cr appearing driven by balance-sheet changes rather than core earnings
A decade of accumulated losses destroyed enormous shareholder value; credibility as a capital allocator is not yet re-established
analysis.detailed_analysis:
IDBI's turnaround from an institution that lost INR 14,970 Cr in a single year (FY19) to one earning INR 7,656 Cr in FY25 is operationally commendable. Credit goes to the resolution of legacy NPAs and tighter underwriting. However, I do not buy banks for their recoveries — I buy them for their future compounding ability, and here IDBI falls short. Revenue in FY25 (INR 28,917 Cr) is barely above FY16 levels (INR 28,058 Cr); a franchise that cannot grow revenues over a full economic cycle has no durable competitive edge.

The 94.72% promoter concentration means this is effectively still a government bank in terms of strategic decision-making. The promised strategic divestiture has dragged on through multiple budget cycles with no resolution. At P/B of 1.16x, the stock is not expensive in absolute terms, but I require both quality and a sensible price — and this bank does not yet demonstrate the consistent returns on equity that define a business worth owning for the long run.
